title: The Red Hunter and the Drummers

pages.text: At the edge of Yendi, Sulemana and Zuwera sat before Elder Mahama. Beside him stood a drum shaped like an hourglass. “In Dagbon, drummers keep our history,” he said. “They are called the Lunsi. They remember the names of kings and the stories of our people, and they sing them. I will tell you what the drummers tell.”
sentences: At the edge of Yendi, Sulemana and Zuwera sat before Elder Mahama.
Beside him stood a drum shaped like an hourglass.
“In Dagbon, drummers keep our history,” he said.
“They are called the Lunsi.
They remember the names of kings and the stories of our people, and they sing them.
I will tell you what the drummers tell.”
pages.alt: Two children sit before an elder who rests a hand on an hourglass drum.

pages.text: “The drummers begin with a hunter called Tohazie, the Red Hunter,” said Elder Mahama. “He was a brave man and a great hunter, and the story says he came from far away. When he reached a village in need, he helped its people, and he married the chief’s daughter. From their family came the line of rulers that later formed the kingdoms of Dagbon, Mamprugu and Nanung.”

“He was a brave man and a great hunter, and the story says he came from far away.
When he reached a village in need, he helped its people, and he married the chief’s daughter.
From their family came the line of rulers that later formed the kingdoms of Dagbon, Mamprugu and Nanung.”
pages.alt: A hunter with a bow stands before a village while elders welcome him.

pages.text: “In one account, Naa Gbewa, a descendant of the Red Hunter, set up a chieftaincy at a place called Pusiga,” said Elder Mahama. “Naa means chief. His sons and daughters became the ancestors of many ruling houses. Tellers do not all agree on the names, or on who came first. That is why you ask more than one person.”

“Naa means chief.
His sons and daughters became the ancestors of many ruling houses.
Tellers do not all agree on the names, or on who came first.
That is why you ask more than one person.”
pages.alt: A chief on a skin stool at Pusiga with several children around him.

pages.text: “Then came a disagreement about who should take the skin, the seat of rule,” said Elder Mahama. “In one account, a son named Tohagu left and founded Mamprugu. Another son, Shitobu, took the skin and became the first Ya-Na, which some also spell Yaa-Naa. The title means king of Dagbon, and the spelling changes with the writer.”

Another son, Shitobu, took the skin and became the first Ya-Na, which some also spell Yaa-Naa.
The title means king of Dagbon, and the spelling changes with the writer.”
pages.alt: Two brothers part ways, one leaving the town while the other sits on a skin stool.

pages.text: “Later, a ruler named Naa Nyagse moved the capital to a place called Yani-Dabari, which means abandoned Yendi,” said Elder Mahama. “Today the king still lives in Yendi, and the royal house is still famous for the drummers who praise its kings. Both the king and the drummers keep our history alive.”

Both the king and the drummers keep our history alive.”
pages.alt: A small walled town with a palace and drummers beside it.

pages.text: “And when did all this happen?” asked Zuwera. “One writer places the ancestors of the kingdom’s rulers after the fall of the old Ghana empire, at the end of the thirteenth century,” said Elder Mahama. “Another says the sons of Naa Gbewa went their separate ways around the fourteenth century. Another gives a reign for Naa Nyagse of 1416 to 1432. The drummers do not give year numbers.”

The drummers do not give year numbers.”
pages.alt: A timeline with dates for the thirteenth century and the fourteenth century and a question mark.

pages.text: “There are people older than the kings,” said Elder Mahama. “They are called the Tindaamba, the earth priests. They are chosen by an oracle, not by the king, and they still lead many sacred rites. Their place in our story reminds us that the land and its keepers were here first.”

“They are called the Tindaamba, the earth priests.
They are chosen by an oracle, not by the king, and they still lead many sacred rites.
Their place in our story reminds us that the land and its keepers were here first.”
pages.alt: An earth priest stands on a hill with a bowl of water and a staff.

pages.text: “So how do we know what is true?” asked Sulemana. “We listen to the drummers, to the elders and to the writers, and we ask whether they agree,” said Elder Mahama. “Some parts are tradition and cannot be tested. Some can be checked. Ask permission before you record a drummer. These histories belong to Dagbon.” Zuwera nodded. The drum began to speak. The end.

pages.alt: The children listen as the drummer begins to play, with the elder smiling beside them.

activities.question: Who keeps the history of Dagbon in the story?

activities.prompt: Elder Mahama says “ask more than one person”. Why?
options: Because one person is never enough to talk

activities.question: What do the dates show about this history?
options: Writers do not agree on when it happened

activities.definition: The office or rule of a chief.

activities.prompt: Put the drummers’ account in order.
items: A hunter called Tohazie arrived and married the chief’s daughter.
Naa Gbewa set up a chieftaincy.
Sons and daughters became ancestors of ruling houses.
A ruler moved the capital to a place that became Yendi.

activities.prompt: Whose stories do you want to keep safe for the future?

glossary.definition: The office or rule of a chief.
A person who comes from a particular ancestor.
A person or object through which people believe they receive guidance from the spirits.
The main town or city where a ruler lives.
People who play drums, sometimes keeping history by memory.
